newsitem.title: JAPAN: Iraq attack could push Asian crude rally further.
newsitem.headline: Iraq attack could push Asian crude rally further.

text.p: Crude oil prices in Asia jumped on Tuesday after the United States launched a missile attack on Iraq and traders said the rally could have further to go.

One economist said West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude prices, a benchmark traded on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX), could reach $30 per barrel, a level not seen since October 1990 after Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in August that year.
Others traders were less bullish and suggested, barring a fresh escalation of hostilities, that prices were more likely to trade up to $25 per barrel at the most.

The NYMEX October contract, which trades in Asia on a screen-based system called ACCESS, touched a high of $24.00 per barrel after news around 0558 GMT that the United States had launched cruise missiles against Iraqi air defence targets.
The Pentagon said the missiles were launched in retaliation for Iraqi military attacks against Kurds.
By 0803 GMT the October NYMEX contract last traded at $23.90, up from the New York close on Friday of $22.25. New York markets were closed on Monday for the Labor Day holiday.
"I think the price of crude could jump over $30 a barrel in the case of WTI," said Kazuaki Kondo, senior economist at the Japanese Institute of Middle Eastern Economies.
The missile attacks followed several days of rising tension after Iraqi forces moved into Kurdish-held opposition territory.
A Western defence source said B-52 bombers launched 25 to 30 missiles at military targets in southern Iraq.
One oil company trader said he thought the confrontation between the U.S. and Iraq would be short-lived.
"I think the market's being level-headed about the news," he said and predicted NYMEX October crude would rise no higher than $24 or $25 per barrel.
He said the market would need a major escalation in hostilities for prices to take off.
The key front month contract on NYMEX reached as high as $41.15 in October 1990. Brent North Sea crude oil reached $40.95 the same month.

Brent prices trading on the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX) rose to $23.50 after the missile attack, up from a London Brent close on Monday of $21.99. October Brent closed on SIMEX at $22.50.
Crude oil traders said the price rise was also supported by the United Nations' move to put a $2 billion Iraqi oil-for-food deal on hold.
Traders had expected Iraqi oil exports of as much as 700,000 barrels per day to start during September.

In addition, petroleum stocks in the United States, especially heating oil and gasoline, are at very low levels which adds to worries that Middle East hostilities could result in a break in the crude supply chain.

"Prices will most likely ease in two to three days," one trader said. "The developments will not effect the supply/demand situation, the supply/demand situation will just return to before the agreement on the partial Iraqi oil sales."

Another trader said: "We will watch the situation calmly and carefully. We were not waiting with baited breath for Iraqi oil to enter the market. Talks on Iraqi oil sales had not yet reached that final stage."
Asian product prices also rallied on Tuesday.

Singapore gas oil derivative swaps, a hedging instrument, rose to a five-year high of $27.85 per barrel and naphtha swaps trading in Singapore were quoted at $20.90, the highest level in at least two years, traders said.
